A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ACCORD, with matching authors, core losses, and personalization tasks. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, including equations, tables, and figures, allowing content to be matched across revisions and relocations.

before.justification: V1 reports original DreamBench, StyleBench, and FFHQ experiments, quantitative loss ablations, and generated-image comparisons in the main text and appendix.

after.justification: V2 retains original personalization experiments and adds human evaluations, further ablations, a hamster personalization experiment, and computation and memory measurements.

M1.justification: The operational losses remain unchanged: DDLoss uses the same conditional denoising comparisons, timestep weighting, and stopped gradients; PDLoss matches personalized and superclass cosine similarities. The revised PDLoss justification and additional backbone evaluations do not establish a changed algorithm.

E1.justification: DreamBench subject personalization, StyleBench style personalization, and FFHQ face personalization are retained. V2 Appendix A.5 adds evaluation on self-collected hamster photographs, extending the data coverage within the existing subject-personalization task.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 adds evaluated DreamBench comparators CoRe-SD1.5, SVDiff, and OmniGen; Table 2 adds OmniGen and B-LoRA to StyleBench comparisons. These substantially broaden the actual comparator set. SVDiff was cited in v1 but was absent from its reported comparisons.

E3.justification: The main LoRA comparisons switch from SD1.5 to SDXL, while some SD1.5 results remain in v2 Table 3; FLUX configurations are also added. New protocols include randomized, anonymized human comparisons totaling 1,800 responses, one/three/all-reference-image evaluations, and controlled resource measurements using batch size 4 and 1,000 steps on H100.

E4.justification: V2 adds DDLoss-only VisualEncoder ablations, FLUX evaluations, reference-image-count sensitivity, a nine-combination loss-weight study, and another alternative PDLoss objective (Tables 3, 4, 6, and 8). Appendix A.6.2 adds concrete failure cases. The dependence-discrepancy curves already present in v1 are retained and relocated.

E5.justification: V2 Table 1 introduces inter-annotator percent agreement for the human evaluation, adding a measure of judgment reliability absent from v1. Neither version reports repeated-seed variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial numerical and qualitative evidence for new comparators, human preferences, ablations, resource costs, and hamster personalization. For example, Table 9 reports hamster CLIP-T of 38.6 versus 39.9 but DINO-I of 59.1 versus 58.6 for LoRA versus ACCORD. Many original DreamBooth, Custom Diffusion, VisualEncoder, and FFHQ scores are unchanged; the replacement main LoRA scores use a different backbone.

T1.justification: Section 3.5 replaces v1's normalized-exponential CLIP Assumption 1 and partition-function argument with an InfoNCE density-ratio lemma, a new approximation in Eq. (10), and Theorem 3 relating PDLoss to conditional-probability differences. This substantially revises the mathematical justification of a central loss. The existing decomposition and DDLoss proofs are largely retained and relocated.

C1.justification: V2 explicitly claims to be the first, or among the first, to formalize concept coupling as statistical dependency. The central contributions otherwise remain the same: two dependence discrepancies, two plug-and-play losses, and improved balance between fidelity and text control, including applicability to zero-shot personalization.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive applicability limits: uncaptured concepts absent from training prompts, dependence on foundation-model capabilities, and incompatibility with non-diffusion autoregressive generators (Appendices A.6.2 and A.11). It also adds interpretations of loss-weight sensitivity, differing gains across baseline families, and computation-versus-quality tradeoffs.

D1.justification: V2 specifies Intern-VL2 and its complete captioning prompt, names A100/H100 hardware, and supplies resource-measurement settings and costs. Existing sampler, inference-step, training-step, and loss-weight guidance is retained. Conversely, v1's face-experiment description of the Q-former and 16 visual tokens is omitted; this is a documentation change, not evidence of an architecture change.

R1.justification: The positioning expands from three regularization families to include region regularization and discussion of closed-source personalization systems. V2 adds substantive comparisons with work such as PaRa, Perfusion, Attend-and-Excite, CoRe, OmniGen, and B-LoRA, plus GPT-4o studies and an InfoNCE theoretical reference. The earlier Specialist Diffusion discussion is removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and related work are extensively rewritten. Separate subject, style, and face experiment sections are consolidated under Personalization Experiments; setup prose is compressed, proofs move into the appendix, and appendix material is reorganized into more focused subsections. These are substantial narrative changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: V2 revises the explanatory diagrams, replaces the compact main qualitative montage with expanded baseline comparisons, and adds human-evaluation columns and several experimental tables. Qualitative panels gain explanatory annotations, while new hamster and failure-case figures expand the visual evidence. Existing discrepancy plots are relocated unchanged, and tables and surrounding text are substantially reflowed.

improvement.justification: Broader comparisons, human judgments, sensitivity tests, and explicit failure and resource analyses improve empirical scrutiny and practical transparency over v1. However, the revised PDLoss argument replaces an explicit softmax assumption with an insufficiently justified identification of cosine similarity with a density ratio in Eq. (10). V2 also claims improvements across all metrics despite lower CLIP-T in Table 6. These weaknesses temper the expanded evidence and documentation to a limited net quality improvement.
